name: Synthetic Long Put
summary: 100 short shares plus one long call at the same strike replicates a long put; used when the put is expensive relative to the call plus carry.

legs.strike_rule: n/a — short 100 shares at market (requires locate/borrow)
Strike nearest spot, call delta 0.45-0.55, for a true synthetic put

max_profit: (entry_spot x 100) - call_debit if the underlying goes to zero
max_loss: (call_strike - entry_spot) x 100 + call_debit, defined by the long call cap
when_to_use: Only when the listed put prices above the synthetic by more than the borrow cost — i.e. put_ask > (call_ask + strike - spot + borrow_cost). In practice on a retail account this is almost never true, because retail borrow rates are far worse than the market-maker rates embedded in option prices.
entry_rules: NOT PRACTICALLY VIABLE on Alpaca paper, and marginal on live retail. Requires shorting 100 shares, which needs an available borrow, incurs a borrow fee the options market has already priced in more cheaply, and exposes the account to buy-in risk. The correct implementation for this account is: just buy the put.
Options side is Level 2 (long call only). The blocking constraint is the short stock leg, not the options approval.
If ever run: only when put_ask - (call_ask + strike - spot) > annualised_borrow_rate x strike x T/365 + 0.10, and only on a name with a borrow rate under 1% annualised.
Alpaca paper fills short-stock orders on names that may be hard or impossible to borrow live — a backtest or paper result here does not transfer to production. Flag any fill as unvalidated.
management_rules: Treat as a long put: close at 50% of the maximum theoretical gain or at a 50% loss of the call debit.
Monitor the borrow fee daily; if the annualised rate rises above 5%, close the structure — the carry will eat the edge that justified it.
If the shares are bought in by the broker, the long call becomes an unhedged directional bet and must be closed the same session.
exit_rules: No short option legs, so no assignment risk from options.

The long call must be closed by 15:40 ET on expiration day if ITM: auto-exercise would buy 100 shares to cover the short, which may be the desired outcome but must be an explicit decision, not an accident.
Close the short shares and the long call as a single package; never unwind one side and leave the other.
If the underlying announces a dividend, the short stock position owes the dividend — close before the ex-date unless the dividend is explicitly budgeted.
assignment_risk: No option assignment risk (no short options). The equivalent hazard is on the stock leg: a hard-to-borrow buy-in can force the short to be covered at any time, at any price, with no notice.
buying_power: Reg T short stock: 50% of the short proceeds held as margin, plus the call debit. Roughly $5,000 plus $300 on a $100 underlying, plus ongoing borrow fees.
liquidity_needs: Easy-to-borrow status is the real requirement. Call OI >= 250.
common_mistakes: Building this because the short-stock view exists anyway, and forgetting that the long call is a decaying asset that must be rolled. Also assuming paper-trading borrow availability reflects reality.
zero_dte_notes: Pointless at 0DTE — the overnight borrow cost and the share settlement mechanics dwarf any one-day edge.
